rows.subtopic: Coulomb's Law and Forces Between Multiple Charges
rows.stem: Two charges \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) are placed at the centres of two spherical conducting shells of radius \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) respectively. The shells are arranged such that their centres are \(d\,[\,>(r_1 + r_2)]\) distance apart. The force on \(q_2\) due to \(q_1\) is :
rows.solution: The two shells are CONDUCTING, and a conductor screens its own cavity: the electric field inside a hollow conductor, due to any charges lying outside it, is zero. So the field of \(q_1\) — together with the field of all the charges it induces on the first shell — does not penetrate into the cavity of the second shell at all. The only charges left to act on \(q_2\) are those induced on the inner surface of its own shell, and because \(q_2\) sits exactly at the centre that induced charge is distributed with perfect spherical symmetry about it, so it pulls equally in every direction and contributes nothing either. The net force on \(q_2\) is therefore zero, which is the choice 'Zero'. The Coulomb expressions offered would apply only to two bare point charges in free space, with no conducting shells in between.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: An electron enters a uniform magnetic field with speed \(v\). It describes a semicircular path and comes out of the field. The final speed of the electron is :
rows.solution: The magnetic force on a moving charge is \(\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\), which is always perpendicular to the velocity. A force perpendicular to the displacement does NO work, so the kinetic energy of the electron cannot change while it is inside the field — only the direction of its velocity changes, which is exactly why the path bends into a semicircle of radius \(r = mv/eB\). The electron therefore leaves the field with the same speed it entered with, matching the choice \(v\).

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Properties of Materials
rows.stem: The magnetic field lines near a substance are as shown in the figure. The substance is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem names no property of the substance, so what the drawn lines DO around it is the entire question. Described: a plain horizontal rectangle representing the substance, with magnetic field lines running past it from left to right, several carrying arrowheads. Withheld: whether the lines crowd into the block or are pushed out around it — that is exactly what discriminates the four listed materials. Page idx 4.
rows.solution: In the figure the field lines do not pass through the block: they are pushed OUT of it and bulge around it, so the flux density inside the substance is less than it is outside. Expulsion of magnetic flux like this is the signature of a DIAMAGNETIC material, for which the relative permeability is slightly less than \(1\) and the susceptibility is small and negative. Of the four substances listed, copper is diamagnetic. Sodium and aluminium are paramagnetic, so the lines would crowd slightly INTO the block, and iron is ferromagnetic, so they would be drawn into it very strongly indeed. The substance is therefore copper.

rows.subtopic: AC Voltage Applied to a Resistor
rows.stem: The figure shows variation of current (I) with time (t) in four devices P, Q, R and S. The device in which an alternating current flows is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — all four options are simply the curve LABELS, so the curves are the question. Described: a single set of axes, vertical axis I, horizontal axis t, origin marked 0, carrying four separate curves labelled P, Q, R and S, plus one dashed horizontal reference line. Withheld: the SHAPE of each of the four curves and where each sits relative to the t-axis. Page idx 4.
rows.solution: An alternating current is one that periodically REVERSES its direction, so on a graph of \(I\) against \(t\) it must cross the time axis and take negative values as well as positive ones. Curve P does oscillate, but about the dashed line well above the axis, so the current never falls to zero or reverses — that is a pulsating direct current. Curves Q and R rise steadily and stay positive throughout, so those are direct currents too, one growing uniformly and the other growing at a falling rate. Only curve S swings alternately above and below the \(t\)-axis, reversing its direction every half period. So the device in which an alternating current flows is S.

rows.subtopic: Electromagnetic Spectrum
rows.stem: The electromagnetic waves used in radar systems are :
rows.solution: Radar has to send out a narrow, well-defined beam, bounce it off a distant object such as an aircraft or a ship, and time the echo. That demands waves whose wavelength is short compared with the target — of the order of millimetres to centimetres — so that they are not appreciably diffracted around it and can be beamed in a single direction. Microwaves have exactly that wavelength range. Infrared is strongly absorbed and scattered by the atmosphere, ultraviolet more so, and X-rays are ionising and would pass through or be absorbed rather than reflected usefully. So the waves used in radar systems are microwaves.

rows.subtopic: Interference and Young's Experiment
rows.stem: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the fringe width is found to be \(\beta\). If the entire apparatus is immersed in a liquid of refractive index \(\mu\), the new fringe width will be :
rows.solution: The fringe width in a double-slit experiment is \(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\). Immersing the whole apparatus in a liquid changes neither the slit separation \(d\) nor the slit-to-screen distance \(D\), and it cannot change the frequency of the light, which is fixed by the source. What it does change is the wavelength: in a medium of refractive index \(\mu\) the speed falls to \(c/\mu\), so \(\lambda' = \dfrac{\lambda}{\mu}\). The new fringe width is therefore \(\beta' = \dfrac{\lambda' D}{d} = \dfrac{\lambda D}{\mu d} = \dfrac{\beta}{\mu}\), which is the choice \(\dfrac{\beta}{\mu}\) — the pattern contracts.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: Photons of energy \(3{\cdot}2\) eV are incident on a photosensitive surface. If the stopping potential for the emitted electrons is \(1{\cdot}5\) V, the work function for the surface is :
rows.solution:
By Einstein's photoelectric equation the energy of the incident photon is shared between the work function and the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron, and the stopping potential measures that maximum kinetic energy: \(eV_0 = h
u - \phi_0\). Rearranging, \(\phi_0 = h
u - eV_0\). With the photon energy \(h
u = 3{\cdot}2\) eV and \(eV_0 = 1{\cdot}5\) eV (a stopping potential of \(1{\cdot}5\) V corresponds to \(1{\cdot}5\) eV of kinetic energy), \(\phi_0 = 3{\cdot}2 - 1{\cdot}5 = 1{\cdot}7\) eV. So the work function of the surface is \(1{\cdot}7\) eV.

rows.subtopic: Nuclear Force
rows.stem: Which of the following statements is not true for nuclear forces ?

options.label: A
options.text: They are stronger than Coulomb forces.

options.label: B
options.text: They have about the same magnitude for different pairs of nucleons.

options.label: D
options.text: They saturate as the separation between two nucleons increases.

rows.solution: The question asks for the statement that is NOT true. The nuclear force is indeed far stronger than the Coulomb force at nuclear separations, which is what holds protons together in spite of their mutual repulsion; it is charge-independent, so it has about the same magnitude for a neutron-neutron, a neutron-proton and a proton-proton pair; and it is short-ranged and saturating, a nucleon interacting only with its immediate neighbours. Those three statements are all correct. But the nuclear force is NOT attractive at every separation: it is attractive over the range of about \(0{\cdot}4\) fm to \(2\) fm, and below roughly \(0{\cdot}4\) fm it turns strongly REPULSIVE. That repulsive core is what stops a nucleus from collapsing in on itself and is why nucleons keep a roughly fixed spacing. So the untrue statement is 'They are always attractive.'

rows.subtopic: Lenz's Law and Conservation of Energy
rows.stem: The direction of induced current in the loop abc is :

options.label: C
options.text: along abc if I is constant

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem names neither the loop's position nor the current's sense, and every option is a directed answer. Described: a closed loop drawn ABOVE a long straight wire, its points labelled a at the left, b at the right and c inside at the bottom; the wire runs between end labels x and y and carries a current labelled I marked by an arrowhead. Withheld: which way that arrowhead points. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The long wire carries the current \(I\) from x to y, that is, to the right, and the loop lies ABOVE it. By the right-hand rule the magnetic field of the wire in the region above it points OUT of the page, so the flux threading the loop is outward.

If \(I\) increases, that outward flux increases. By Lenz's law the induced current must oppose the change, so it must set up a flux INTO the page inside the loop, which requires it to circulate CLOCKWISE as the figure is drawn. With a at the left of the loop, b at the right and c at the bottom, the path a to b to c and back to a is precisely that clockwise circulation. So the induced current flows along abc when \(I\) increases.

(Were \(I\) instead decreasing, the induced current would run the other way round, along acb; and a constant \(I\) gives a constant flux, hence no emf and no induced current at all.)

rows.subtopic: AC Voltage Applied to an Inductor and a Capacitor
rows.stem: An ac voltage \(v = v_0 \sin \omega t\) is applied to a series combination of a resistor R and an element X. The instantaneous current in the circuit is \(I = I_0 \sin\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\). Then which of the following is correct ?

options.label: B
options.text: X is an inductor and \(X_L = R\)

options.label: D
options.text: X is a capacitor and \(X_C = R\)

rows.solution:
Compare the two expressions: the applied voltage is \(v = v_0 \sin \omega t\) while the current is \(I = I_0 \sin\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\). The current therefore LEADS the voltage by \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

In a series combination of a resistor with an inductor the current lags the voltage; in a series combination with a capacitor it leads. So the element X must be a capacitor.

For a series \(RC\) circuit the phase angle satisfies \(\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_C}{R}\). Here \(\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), so \(\tan\phi = 1\) and hence \(X_C = R\). So X is a capacitor whose reactance equals the resistance, \(X_C = R\).

rows.subtopic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves
rows.stem: A plane wavefront is incident on a concave mirror of radius of curvature R. The radius of the refracted wavefront will be :
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: this question was VOIDED for the English-medium paper. The scheme's Section-A entry reads: '(c) \(\dfrac{R}{2}\) for students who have opted to answer the question in Hindi medium only. English medium students - There is misprint in the English version of the question as the word "reflected" appear as "refracted". Therefore full mark to be awarded to each student who have opted to answer the question in English medium.' So the letter (c) is the HINDI answer, and every English-medium candidate was given the mark whatever was written.]

As the question is printed here it asks for the 'refracted' wavefront produced by a concave MIRROR. A mirror reflects light; it does not refract it, so there is no refracted wavefront and none of the four values can be correct. That is why no answer is stored for this row.

The question CBSE intended is the REFLECTED wavefront, and it is worth working through. A plane wavefront striking a concave mirror of radius of curvature \(R\) is reflected as a converging spherical wavefront that closes in on the principal focus, which lies at \(f = \dfrac{R}{2}\) from the pole. The centre of curvature of the reflected wavefront is therefore the focus, and at the moment it leaves the mirror its radius is the pole-to-focus distance, \(\dfrac{R}{2}\) — the value accepted in the Hindi version.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Wave Nature of Matter
rows.stem: A proton and an alpha particle have the same kinetic energy. The ratio of de Broglie wavelengths associated with the proton to that with the alpha particle is :
rows.solution:
The de Broglie wavelength is \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\), and a particle of mass \(m\) with kinetic energy \(K\) has momentum \(p = \sqrt{2mK}\). Hence \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}\).

The proton and the alpha particle are given the SAME kinetic energy, so \(K\) cancels and \(\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\):

\(\dfrac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_\alpha} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_\alpha}{m_p}}\).

An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, of mass four times the proton mass, so \(\dfrac{m_\alpha}{m_p} = 4\) and \(\dfrac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_\alpha} = \sqrt{4} = 2\). The required ratio is \(2\).

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: The potential energy of an electron in the second excited state in hydrogen atom is :
rows.solution:
The ground state is \(n = 1\), the first excited state \(n = 2\), so the SECOND excited state is \(n = 3\).

The total energy of the electron in the \(n\)th Bohr orbit of hydrogen is \(E_n = -\dfrac{13{\cdot}6}{n^2}\) eV, so \(E_3 = -\dfrac{13{\cdot}6}{3^2} = -1{\cdot}51\) eV.

In the Bohr atom the electron is bound by an inverse-square force, so the virial theorem applies: the potential energy is twice the total energy (equivalently, it is minus twice the kinetic energy), \(U = 2E\). Hence

\(U_3 = 2 \times (-1{\cdot}51) = -3{\cdot}02\) eV.

So the potential energy in the second excited state is \(-3{\cdot}02\) eV. (The value \(-1{\cdot}51\) eV offered among the choices is the TOTAL energy of that state, not the potential energy, and \(-3{\cdot}4\) eV is the total energy of the FIRST excited state.)

rows.subtopic: Mass-Energy and Nuclear Binding Energy
rows.stem: The difference in mass of \(^{7}\mathrm{X}\) nucleus and total mass of its constituent nucleons is \(21{\cdot}00\) u. The binding energy per nucleon for this nucleus is equal to the energy equivalent of :
rows.solution:
The 'difference in mass of the nucleus and the total mass of its constituent nucleons' is the mass defect, \(\Delta m = 21{\cdot}00\) u, and the binding energy of the nucleus is the energy equivalent of that mass defect, \(B = \Delta m\,c^2\).

The nucleus \(^{7}\mathrm{X}\) has mass number \(A = 7\), so it contains \(7\) nucleons. The binding energy per nucleon is therefore the energy equivalent of

\(\dfrac{\Delta m}{A} = \dfrac{21{\cdot}00}{7} = 3\) u.

So the binding energy per nucleon equals the energy equivalent of \(3\) u.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: The threshold voltage for a p-n junction diode used in the circuit is \(0{\cdot}7\) V. The type of biasing and current in the circuit are :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem says only 'the circuit', and every option names a biasing sense. Described: one closed series loop containing a diode labelled D, a resistor labelled 100 \(\Omega\) and a cell labelled \(0{\cdot}5\) V. Withheld: the diode's orientation relative to the cell's polarity, which is precisely what decides forward versus reverse biasing and hence the answer. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
Two things have to be settled: the sense of the biasing, and whether the diode actually conducts.

In the circuit drawn, the cell drives conventional current round the loop in the direction in which the diode will pass it — from its p-side to its n-side — so the diode is FORWARD biased.

But a junction diode does not conduct appreciably as soon as it is forward biased. Until the applied forward voltage exceeds the threshold (knee) voltage, the barrier potential of the junction is not overcome and the current stays negligibly small. Here the threshold voltage is \(0{\cdot}7\) V while the cell supplies only \(0{\cdot}5\) V, which is less than the threshold. The diode therefore does not conduct and the current in the circuit is zero.

So the biasing is forward and the current is \(0\) A. (Had the diode been conducting, the voltage left across the \(100\,\Omega\) resistor would have driven a current of a few milliamperes, which is where the milliampere values among the choices come from.)

rows.subtopic: Electrical Energy and Power
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : When three electric bulbs of power 200 W, 100 W and 50 W are connected in series to a source, the power consumed by the 50 W bulb is maximum.
Reason (R) : In a series circuit, current is the same through each bulb, but the potential difference across each bulb is different.
rows.context: Questions number 16 to 18 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
Take the Assertion first. Bulbs are rated at a common supply voltage, so a bulb of rated power \(P\) has resistance \(R = \dfrac{V^2}{P}\) — the SMALLER the rated power, the LARGER the resistance. The \(50\) W bulb therefore has the greatest resistance and the \(200\) W bulb the least. Joined in series they all carry the same current \(I\), and the power each one actually consumes is \(P = I^2R\), which is greatest for the greatest resistance. So the \(50\) W bulb does consume the most power, and the Assertion is true.

The Reason is also a true statement: in a series circuit the current is common to all the elements while the potential difference divides between them in proportion to their resistances.

But it is not a complete explanation of the Assertion. It stops at saying the potential differences differ; it never supplies the two steps that actually settle the question, namely that \(R = \dfrac{V^2}{P}\) puts the resistances in the reverse order of the rated powers, and that with a common current the consumed power goes as \(I^2R\). So both statements are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.subtopic: Torque on a Current Loop and Magnetic Dipole
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : A current carrying square loop made of a wire of length L is placed in a magnetic field. It experiences a torque which is greater than the torque on a circular loop made of the same wire carrying the same current in the same magnetic field.
Reason (R) : A square loop occupies more area than a circular loop, both made of wire of the same length.
rows.context: Questions number 16 to 18 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
Both loops are made from the same wire, so both have perimeter \(L\).

Square: side \(\dfrac{L}{4}\), area \(A_{sq} = \left(\dfrac{L}{4}\right)^2 = \dfrac{L^2}{16} = 0{\cdot}0625\,L^2\).

Circle: circumference \(L = 2\pi r\) so \(r = \dfrac{L}{2\pi}\), area \(A_{ci} = \pi r^2 = \dfrac{L^2}{4\pi} = 0{\cdot}0796\,L^2\).

The circle encloses the LARGER area — for a given perimeter it always does, since the circle is the shape of greatest area for a fixed boundary length. The torque on a current loop is \(\tau = NIAB\sin\theta\), which for the same current and the same field is proportional to the area. The CIRCULAR loop therefore experiences the greater torque, not the square one, so the Assertion is false.

The Reason claims the square occupies more area than the circle, which is the opposite of what has just been shown, so the Reason is false as well.

So the Assertion is false and the Reason is also false.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : In 'n' type semiconductor, number density of electrons is greater than the number density of holes but the crystal maintains an overall charge neutrality.
Reason (R) : The charge of electrons donated by donor atoms is just equal and opposite to that of the ionised donor.
rows.context: Questions number 16 to 18 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
In an n-type crystal the added impurity is pentavalent. Four of each donor atom's five valence electrons go into covalent bonds with the neighbouring host atoms; the fifth is bound so weakly that ordinary thermal energy sets it free. The number density of electrons is therefore far greater than the number density of holes, so the Assertion's first clause is true.

Its second clause is true as well, and the Reason is exactly why. Every electron that a donor atom gives up leaves behind that atom as an immobile positive ion fixed in the lattice, carrying a charge equal and opposite to the electron's. The extra mobile negative charge in the crystal is thus matched, atom for atom, by an equal fixed positive charge, so the crystal as a whole stays electrically neutral. Doping supplies carriers; it does not supply net charge.

So both statements are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.subtopic: Electric Dipole and Dipole in a Uniform Field
rows.stem: Two identical dipoles are arranged in x-y plane as shown in the figure. Find the magnitude and the direction of net electric field at the origin O.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem says only 'as shown in the figure', so the charge arrangement IS the data of the question. Described: a pair of axes crossing at a point marked O, with four point charges drawn on them, one on each arm, each at a distance marked a from O and each labelled with a charge; a small separate x-y axis key is drawn to the right. Withheld: which sign sits on which arm, since that fixes both the magnitude and the direction the question asks for. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
Read the arrangement off the figure. On the x-axis there is \(+q\) at \((a, 0)\) and \(-q\) at \((-a, 0)\): that is one dipole, whose moment \(\vec{p_1}\) points from the negative to the positive charge, i.e. along \(+x\). On the y-axis there is \(+q\) at \((0, a)\) and \(-q\) at \((0, -a)\): the second dipole, with \(\vec{p_2}\) along \(+y\). The origin O is the MID-POINT of each dipole.

Field of the first dipole at O. The \(+q\) on the \(+x\) axis pushes the field away from itself, i.e. towards \(-x\), with magnitude \(\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{a^2}\). The \(-q\) on the \(-x\) axis pulls the field towards itself, also towards \(-x\), with the same magnitude. The two add:

\(E_1 = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{a^2}\), directed along OB, that is along \(-x\).

By exactly the same argument the second dipole gives

\(E_2 = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{a^2}\), directed along OD, that is along \(-y\).

The two contributions are equal in magnitude and mutually perpendicular, so they combine to

\(|\vec{E}_{net}| = \sqrt{E_1^2 + E_2^2} = \sqrt{2}\,E_1 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,q}{a^2}\),

and since the two components are equal the resultant bisects them: it points into the third quadrant, at \(45^\circ\) below the negative x-axis, that is at \(225^\circ\) measured from the positive x-axis.

[Note on the marking scheme: its main solution writes '\(|\vec{E_1}| = |\vec{E_2}| = E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{a^2}\)' and then '\(|\vec{E}_{net}| = 2\sqrt{2}\,E\)'. Those two lines are consistent only if \(E\) is read as the field of ONE charge; the field of a whole dipole at its own mid-point is twice that, as shown above. The scheme's final answer, \(\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,q}{a^2}\) at \(225^\circ\), is correct, and its own alternative method — regrouping the four charges as the dipoles CB and AD and using the equatorial field \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}kq}{a^2}\) for each — reproduces it.]

rows.subtopic: Cells, EMF and Internal Resistance
rows.stem: Write two differences between the emf and terminal potential difference of a cell. What is the most important precaution that one should take while drawing current from a cell ?
rows.solution:
Two differences between the emf and the terminal potential difference of a cell:

1. The emf \(\varepsilon\) is the potential difference between the electrodes of the cell on OPEN circuit, when no current is being drawn from it. The terminal potential difference \(V\) is the value between the same two electrodes when the circuit is CLOSED and a current \(I\) is flowing, and then \(V = \varepsilon - Ir\), which is less than the emf.

2. The emf is a fixed property of the cell, decided by the chemical nature of its electrodes and electrolyte; it does not depend on the external resistance or on the internal resistance \(r\). The terminal potential difference depends on both — it falls as the current drawn increases, and it rises towards \(\varepsilon\) only as \(I\) tends to zero.

The most important precaution: always draw the current THROUGH a suitable external resistance connected in series, so that the current stays well below the short-circuit value \(\dfrac{\varepsilon}{r}\). In other words, never short-circuit the cell. With \(R = 0\) the whole of \(\varepsilon I\) is dissipated inside the cell itself as \(I^2 r\), which overheats it and damages it permanently.

rows.subtopic: The Bar Magnet
rows.stem:
A small magnetised needle P is placed at the origin of x-y plane with its magnetic moment pointing along the y-axis. Another identical magnetised needle Q is placed in two positions, one by one.
Case 1 : at (a, 0) with its magnetic moment pointing along x-axis.
Case 2 : at (0, a) with its magnetic moment pointing along y-axis.
(a) In which case is the potential energy of P and Q minimum ?
(b) In which case is P and Q not in equilibrium ?
Justify your answers.
rows.solution:
The needle P sits at the origin with its magnetic moment along the y-axis, so the field it produces at another point depends on where that point lies relative to its own axis.

Case 1: Q is at \((a, 0)\). That point lies on the perpendicular bisector of P — its EQUATORIAL line — where P's field is ANTIPARALLEL to P's own moment, i.e. along \(-y\), of magnitude \(B_{eq} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{M}{a^3}\). But Q's moment points along \(+x\), perpendicular to this field. So \(U = -MB\cos 90^\circ = 0\), and the torque is \(\tau = MB\sin 90^\circ = MB\), the largest it can be.

Case 2: Q is at \((0, a)\). That point lies on the AXIS of P, where P's field is ALONG P's moment, i.e. along \(+y\), of magnitude \(B_{ax} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2M}{a^3}\). Q's moment also points along \(+y\), parallel to the field. So \(U = -MB_{ax}\cos 0^\circ = -MB_{ax}\), which is negative, and \(\tau = MB_{ax}\sin 0^\circ = 0\).

(a) The potential energy is minimum in CASE 2. Since \(U = -MB\cos\theta\), the energy is least when \(\theta = 0^\circ\), and Case 2 is the arrangement in which Q's moment lies along the direction of the field of P. That is also the orientation of stable equilibrium.

(b) P and Q are NOT in equilibrium in CASE 1. There Q sits on the normal bisector of P, so the two moments are mutually perpendicular; each needle then experiences the maximum torque \(\tau = MB\sin 90^\circ = MB\) and will turn. In Case 2 the torque is zero, so that pair is in equilibrium.

rows.subtopic: Displacement Current
rows.stem: What is a displacement current ? How is it different from a conduction current ?
rows.solution:
A displacement current is the current attributed to a CHANGING ELECTRIC FLUX in a region of space — for instance in the empty gap between the plates of a capacitor while it is being charged, where no charge crosses from one plate to the other yet a magnetic field is undoubtedly present. Maxwell defined it as

\(i_d = \varepsilon_0 \dfrac{d\phi_E}{dt}\),

where \(\phi_E\) is the electric flux through the surface concerned. Its purpose is to make Ampere's circuital law consistent: the total current \(i_c + i_d\) is continuous everywhere, even across a capacitor gap.

How it differs from a conduction current. A conduction current \(I = \dfrac{dq}{dt}\) is an actual transport of charge — free electrons drifting through a conductor — and it therefore needs a material medium containing mobile charges. A displacement current involves NO motion of charge at all; it exists wherever the electric field, and hence the electric flux, is changing with time, including in vacuum. What the two have in common is their magnetic effect: each produces a magnetic field in exactly the same way, which is why they can be added together in Ampere's law.

rows.subtopic: Electromagnetic Waves and their Properties
rows.stem: Write any two characteristics of an electromagnetic wave. Why are microwaves used in radar systems ?
rows.solution:
Any two characteristics of an electromagnetic wave:

1. It needs no material medium for its propagation, and travels through free space with the speed \(c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} = 3 \times 10^8\) m/s.

2. It is TRANSVERSE: the oscillating electric field \(\vec{E}\), the oscillating magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) and the direction of propagation are mutually perpendicular. The two fields oscillate in phase with \(E_0 = cB_0\), and the energy of the wave is shared equally between the electric and the magnetic field.

Why microwaves are used in radar systems: their wavelengths are short — of the order of millimetres to centimetres — and therefore small compared with the targets radar has to detect. Short wavelengths are not appreciably diffracted around such objects, so a microwave beam can be sent out in a single well-defined direction, travels in a straight line, and is reflected back by the target. Timing the returning echo then gives the target's range, and the direction in which the beam was pointed gives its bearing.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: The figure shows \(v_m^2\) versus \(\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\) graph for photoelectrons emitted from a surface where \(v_m\) is the maximum speed of electrons and \(\lambda\) is the wavelength of incident radiation. Using this graph and Einstein's photoelectric equation, obtain the expression for Planck's constant and work function of the surface.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem instructs the student to use THIS graph, and the slope and intercept it carries are what the answer is built from. Described: a pair of axes, vertical axis \(v_m^2\), horizontal axis \(\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\), origin marked O, one straight line crossing the horizontal axis with its portion below that axis drawn dashed, and the angle the line makes with the axis marked \(\theta\). Withheld: nothing further is drawn. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
Einstein's photoelectric equation, written for radiation of wavelength \(\lambda\) so that the photon energy is \(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\), is

\(\dfrac{1}{2}mv_m^2 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi_0\).

Rearranging it so that the plotted quantities appear explicitly,

\(v_m^2 = \left(\dfrac{2hc}{m}\right)\dfrac{1}{\lambda} - \dfrac{2\phi_0}{m}\).

This has the form \(y = (\text{slope})x + (\text{intercept})\) with \(y = v_m^2\) and \(x = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}\), so the graph of \(v_m^2\) against \(\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\) is a straight line, which is what the figure shows. Comparing term by term:

slope \(= \dfrac{2hc}{m} = \tan\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle marked between the line and the \(\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\) axis;

intercept on the \(v_m^2\) axis \(= -\dfrac{2\phi_0}{m}\), which is NEGATIVE — that is why the line meets the \(\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\) axis at a positive value and the portion below the axis is drawn dashed.

The slope and the intercept can both be read off the graph, so:

Planck's constant, \(h = \dfrac{m}{2c} \times \text{slope} = \dfrac{m}{2c}\tan\theta\);

Work function, \(\phi_0 = \dfrac{m}{2} \times |\text{intercept on the } v_m^2 \text{ axis}|\),

where \(m\) is the mass of the electron and \(c\) the speed of light.

rows.subtopic: Nuclear Energy
rows.stem: Draw the graph showing the variation of binding energy per nucleon with mass number A of nuclei \((2 < A < 170)\). Use this graph to explain the release of energy in nuclear fission.
rows.solution:
Graph to be drawn: binding energy per nucleon \(\dfrac{B}{A}\) (in MeV) on the vertical axis against mass number \(A\) on the horizontal axis. The curve starts very low for the lightest nuclei (about \(1{\cdot}1\) MeV for \(^{2}\mathrm{H}\)), climbs steeply through \(^{4}\mathrm{He}\), \(^{6}\mathrm{Li}\), \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\) and \(^{16}\mathrm{O}\), reaches a broad flat maximum of about \(8{\cdot}8\) MeV near \(A = 56\) (iron), and then falls away slowly, reaching about \(7{\cdot}6\) MeV for the heaviest nuclei. Full marks are awarded even if the numerical values are not marked on the axes.

Using the graph to explain fission. A very heavy nucleus lies on the slowly FALLING part of the curve, so its nucleons are comparatively loosely bound — about \(7{\cdot}6\) MeV each. When such a nucleus splits into two fragments of roughly half its mass, those fragments lie much nearer the peak of the curve, where the binding energy per nucleon is about \(8{\cdot}4\) MeV. The nucleons in the products are therefore MORE tightly bound than they were in the parent.

Since a more tightly bound system has lower energy, the excess must be released. The gain is roughly \(0{\cdot}8\) MeV per nucleon, and with about \(240\) nucleons taking part this amounts to of the order of \(200\) MeV liberated in a single fission — which appears mainly as the kinetic energy of the fragments.

rows.subtopic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges
rows.stem: Obtain an expression for electrostatic potential energy of a system of three charges \(q\), \(2q\) and \(-3q\) placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side \(a\).
rows.solution:
The electrostatic potential energy of a system of point charges is the total work that must be done to assemble them from infinity, and it is the sum of the energies of every PAIR:

\(U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r_{12}}\) for one pair.

Here the three charges \(q\), \(2q\) and \(-3q\) sit at the vertices of an equilateral triangle, so every one of the three pairs is separated by the same distance \(a\). Summing over the pairs \((q, 2q)\), \((2q, -3q)\) and \((-3q, q)\):

\(U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{(q)(2q)}{a} + \dfrac{(2q)(-3q)}{a} + \dfrac{(-3q)(q)}{a}\right]\)

\(U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{1}{a}\left[2q^2 - 6q^2 - 3q^2\right]\)

\(U = -\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{7q^2}{a}\).

The result is negative, which says that the attractive pairs outweigh the repulsive one: the system is bound, and work of \(\dfrac{7q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 a}\) would have to be supplied from outside to pull the three charges back to infinity.

rows.subtopic: Electrostatics of Conductors and Dielectrics
rows.stem: Two small conducting balls A and B of radius \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) have charges \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) respectively. They are connected by a wire. Obtain the expression for charges on A and B, in equilibrium.
rows.solution:
Two conditions fix the final charges.

First, charge is CONSERVED. Joining the balls with a wire lets charge flow between them but does not create or destroy any, so if \(q_1'\) and \(q_2'\) are the final charges,

\(q_1' + q_2' = q_1 + q_2 = Q\)   (say).

Second, once the wire is in place the two balls and the wire form a SINGLE conductor, and charge keeps flowing until the whole of it is at one potential. Treating each ball as an isolated sphere of charge on its own surface,

\(V_1 = V_2 \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1'}{r_1} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_2'}{r_2} \Rightarrow \dfrac{q_1'}{r_1} = \dfrac{q_2'}{r_2}\), that is \(q_1' r_2 = q_2' r_1\).

Substituting \(q_2' = Q - q_1'\):

\(q_1' r_2 = (Q - q_1')r_1 \Rightarrow q_1' r_2 + q_1' r_1 = Q r_1 \Rightarrow q_1'(r_1 + r_2) = Q r_1\).

Hence the charges in equilibrium are

\(q_1' = \dfrac{Q r_1}{r_1 + r_2} = \dfrac{(q_1 + q_2) r_1}{r_1 + r_2}\)  and  \(q_2' = Q - q_1' = \dfrac{Q r_2}{r_1 + r_2} = \dfrac{(q_1 + q_2) r_2}{r_1 + r_2}\).

So the total charge redistributes itself in the ratio of the radii, \(q_1' : q_2' = r_1 : r_2\), the bigger ball taking the bigger share.

rows.subtopic: Biot-Savart Law and Field of a Circular Loop
rows.stem: Two circular loops A and B, each of radius 3 m, are placed coaxially at a distance of 4 m. They carry currents of 3 A and 2 A in opposite directions respectively. Find the net magnetic field at the centre of loop A.
rows.solution:
The point in question is the CENTRE of loop A, so loop A contributes its centre field while loop B contributes its axial field at a distance of \(4\) m.

Field at the centre of loop A due to loop A itself, with \(r = 3\) m and \(I = 3\) A:

\(B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 3}{2 \times 3} = 2\pi \times 10^{-7} = 6{\cdot}28 \times 10^{-7}\) T.

Field at the same point due to loop B. That point lies on the axis of loop B at \(x = 4\) m from its centre, with \(R = 3\) m and \(I = 2\) A:

\(B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2 \times 3^2}{2\left(3^2 + 4^2\right)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2 \times 9}{(25)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{36\pi \times 10^{-7}}{125} = 0{\cdot}9 \times 10^{-7}\) T.

Both fields lie along the common axis, but the two currents circulate in OPPOSITE senses, so the two fields point in opposite directions and must be subtracted:

\(B_{net} = B_1 - B_2 = 6{\cdot}28 \times 10^{-7} - 0{\cdot}9 \times 10^{-7} = 5{\cdot}38 \times 10^{-7}\) T,

directed along the axis in the sense of loop A's own field, since the nearer and stronger contribution is that of loop A.

rows.subtopic: Inductance
rows.stem:
(a) The figure shows the variation of induced emf as a function of rate of change of current for two identical solenoids X and Y. One is air cored and the other is iron cored. Which one of them is iron cored ? Why ?
(b) Obtain an expression for self-inductance of a long solenoid of length L and cross-sectional area A having N turns.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (a) is answered by reading the graph; the stem names no slope and no numbers. Described: a pair of axes, vertical axis emf, horizontal axis \(\dfrac{dI}{dt}\), origin marked O, and two straight lines drawn from the origin, labelled X and Y. Withheld: which of the two lines is the steeper, which is the entire discrimination the question tests. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
(a) The emf induced in a coil by a changing current in itself is \(\varepsilon = L\left|\dfrac{dI}{dt}\right|\), so a graph of induced emf against \(\dfrac{dI}{dt}\) is a straight line through the origin whose SLOPE is the self-inductance:

slope \(= \dfrac{\varepsilon}{\left|\dfrac{dI}{dt}\right|} = L\).

In the figure the line labelled X is the steeper of the two, so \(L_X > L_Y\). Now the self-inductance of a solenoid with a core is \(L = \dfrac{\mu_0\mu_r N^2 A}{l}\), and iron has a relative permeability \(\mu_r\) of the order of thousands while air has \(\mu_r \approx 1\). Since the two solenoids are otherwise identical, the iron-cored one must have far the larger inductance. So X is the iron-cored solenoid.

(b) Take a long solenoid of length \(L\), cross-sectional area \(A\) and \(N\) turns, carrying a current \(I\). Because it is long, the field inside is uniform and along the axis:

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{L}\).

The magnetic flux through ONE turn is \(\phi = BA = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I A}{L}\), and since all \(N\) turns are threaded by the same flux, the total flux linkage is

\(\phi_B = N\phi = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{L}I\).

Self-inductance is defined as the flux linkage per unit current, so

self-inductance \(= \dfrac{\phi_B}{I} = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{L}\).

It depends only on the geometry of the solenoid and on the medium filling it; with a core of relative permeability \(\mu_r\) it becomes \(\dfrac{\mu_0\mu_r N^2 A}{L}\).

rows.subtopic: AC Voltage Applied to an Inductor and a Capacitor
rows.stem: A resistor of 30 \(\Omega\) and a capacitor of \(\dfrac{250}{\pi}\) \(\mu\mathrm{F}\) are connected in series to a 200 V, 50 Hz ac source. Calculate (i) the current in the circuit, and (ii) voltage drops across the resistor and the capacitor. (iii) Is the algebraic sum of these voltages more than the source voltage ? If yes, solve the paradox.
rows.solution:
First find the capacitive reactance. The angular frequency is

\(\omega = 2\pi\nu = 2\pi \times 50 = 100\pi\) rad/s,

and with \(C = \dfrac{250}{\pi}\,\mu\mathrm{F} = \dfrac{250}{\pi} \times 10^{-6}\) F,

\(X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{100\pi \times \dfrac{250}{\pi} \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{1}{100 \times 250 \times 10^{-6}} = 40\,\Omega\)

(the \(\pi\) cancels, which is why the capacitance was given in that form).

Impedance of the series \(RC\) circuit:

\(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_C^2} = \sqrt{(30)^2 + (40)^2} = \sqrt{900 + 1600} = 50\,\Omega\).

(i) Current in the circuit:

\(I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z} = \dfrac{200}{50} = 4\) A.

(ii) Voltage drops, the same current passing through both elements:

across the resistor, \(V_R = I_{rms}R = 4 \times 30 = 120\) V;

across the capacitor, \(V_C = I_{rms}X_C = 4 \times 40 = 160\) V.

(iii) Yes — their algebraic sum is \(120 + 160 = 280\) V, which is well above the \(200\) V of the source.

The paradox is only apparent, and it dissolves once the phases are taken into account. These two voltages do not reach their peaks at the same instant, so they may not simply be added as numbers. \(V_R\) is in phase with the current, while \(V_C\) LAGS the current by \(90^\circ\); the two phasors are therefore at right angles and must be combined vectorially:

\(V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + V_C^2} = \sqrt{(120)^2 + (160)^2} = \sqrt{14400 + 25600} = \sqrt{40000} = 200\) V,

which is exactly the source voltage. The instantaneous voltages do always add up to the source voltage; it is only their peak (or rms) values that appear not to.

rows.subtopic: Series LCR Circuit and Resonance
rows.stem: A series LCR circuit with R = 20 \(\Omega\), L = 2 H and C = 50 \(\mu\mathrm{F}\) is connected to a 200 volts ac source of variable frequency. What is (i) the amplitude of the current, and (ii) the average power transferred to the circuit in one complete cycle, at resonance ? (iii) Calculate the potential drop across the capacitor.
rows.solution:
(i) At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal and cancel, so the impedance falls to its minimum value, \(Z = R = 20\,\Omega\). The rms current is then

\(I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{R} = \dfrac{200}{20} = 10\) A,

and the AMPLITUDE of the current is

\(I_0 = \sqrt{2}\,I_{rms} = 1{\cdot}414 \times 10 = 14{\cdot}14\) A.

(ii) At resonance the current is in phase with the applied voltage, so the power factor \(\cos\phi = 1\) and the whole of the power is dissipated in the resistor. Averaged over one complete cycle,

\(P = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi = I_{rms}^2 R = (10)^2 \times 20 = 2000\) W.

(iii) To find the voltage across the capacitor the resonant frequency is needed first:

\(\omega_r = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2 \times 50 \times 10^{-6}}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10^{-4}}} = 100\) rad/s.

Then

\(X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega_r C} = \dfrac{1}{100 \times 50 \times 10^{-6}} = 200\,\Omega\),

and the potential drop across the capacitor is

\(V_C = I_{rms}X_C = 10 \times 200 = 2000\) V.

This is ten times the source voltage, which is not a contradiction: at resonance the voltage across the inductor is equal in magnitude and exactly opposite in phase to this one, so the two cancel and the source needs to supply only the \(200\) V that appears across the resistor. This voltage magnification is the reason a series LCR circuit at resonance is called an acceptor circuit.

rows.subtopic: Diffraction
rows.stem:
(i) In diffraction due to a single slit, the phase difference between light waves reaching a point on the screen is \(5\pi\). Explain whether a bright or a dark fringe will be formed at the point.
(ii) What should the width (a) of each slit be to obtain eight maxima of two double-slit patterns (slit separation d) within the central maximum of the single slit pattern ?
(iii) Draw the plot of intensity distribution in a diffraction pattern due to a single slit.
rows.solution:
(i) In single-slit diffraction the secondary MAXIMA occur where the path difference between the extreme waves is an odd multiple of half a wavelength, that is where the phase difference is

\(\phi = (2n + 1)\pi\),  \(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

Here \(\phi = 5\pi\), and \(5\pi = (2 \times 2 + 1)\pi\) is of exactly that form, with \(n = 2\). So a BRIGHT fringe — a secondary maximum — is formed at the point.

Equivalently, in terms of path difference: \(\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi}\phi = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi} \times 5\pi = \dfrac{5\lambda}{2}\), which is an odd multiple of \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\) and therefore the condition for a secondary maximum (a minimum would need \(\Delta x = n\lambda\), i.e. \(\phi = 2n\pi\)).

(ii) The first diffraction minimum of a slit of width \(a\) lies at \(a\sin\theta = \lambda\), so for small angles \(\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{a}\). The central maximum runs from \(-\dfrac{\lambda}{a}\) to \(+\dfrac{\lambda}{a}\), so its full angular width is \(\dfrac{2\lambda}{a}\).

The interference maxima of the double slit of separation \(d\) are spaced \(\dfrac{\lambda}{d}\) apart in angle. For eight of them to fall inside the central diffraction maximum, eight of those spacings must fill that angular width:

\(8 \times \dfrac{\lambda}{d} = \dfrac{2\lambda}{a} \Rightarrow \dfrac{8}{d} = \dfrac{2}{a} \Rightarrow a = \dfrac{d}{4}\).

So each slit should be one quarter of the slit separation wide.

(iii) Plot to be drawn: intensity \(I\) on the vertical axis against \(\theta\) (or against position on the screen) on the horizontal. It shows one very tall CENTRAL maximum centred on \(\theta = 0\), of twice the width of the others, dropping to zero at \(a\sin\theta = \pm\lambda, \pm 2\lambda, \pm 3\lambda, \ldots\); between consecutive zeros lie secondary maxima, symmetric about the centre, whose heights fall away rapidly on either side (the first is only about \(4\%\) of the central peak).

rows.subtopic: Interference and Young's Experiment
rows.stem:
(i) In a Young's double-slit experiment \(\mathrm{SS_2} - \mathrm{SS_1} = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}\), where \(\mathrm{S_1}\) and \(\mathrm{S_2}\) are the two slits as shown in the figure. Find the path difference \((\mathrm{S_2P} - \mathrm{S_1P})\) for constructive and destructive interference at P.
(ii) What is the effect on the interference fringes in a Young's double-slit experiment, if the monochromatic source S is replaced by a source of white light ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (i) says 'as shown in the figure' and the geometry it fixes is what the path difference is computed from. Described: three vertical screens drawn in a row — a source slit labelled S on the left, a double slit carrying S\(_1\) above S\(_2\) in the middle, and an observation screen on the right with a point P marked on it. Withheld: the vertical positions of S, S\(_1\), S\(_2\) and P relative to one another. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
(i) The waves arriving at P have travelled by the routes S to \(\mathrm{S_1}\) to P and S to \(\mathrm{S_2}\) to P, so the TOTAL path difference is made up of two parts — the difference created before the slits and the difference created after them:

\(\Delta x = (\mathrm{SS_2} + \mathrm{S_2P}) - (\mathrm{SS_1} + \mathrm{S_1P}) = (\mathrm{SS_2} - \mathrm{SS_1}) + (\mathrm{S_2P} - \mathrm{S_1P})\).

The question gives \(\mathrm{SS_2} - \mathrm{SS_1} = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}\), so

\(\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{4} + (\mathrm{S_2P} - \mathrm{S_1P})\).

For CONSTRUCTIVE interference the total path difference must be a whole number of wavelengths, \(\Delta x = n\lambda\):

\(\dfrac{\lambda}{4} + (\mathrm{S_2P} - \mathrm{S_1P}) = n\lambda \Rightarrow \mathrm{S_2P} - \mathrm{S_1P} = n\lambda - \dfrac{\lambda}{4} = \left(n - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)\lambda\),  \(n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\)

For DESTRUCTIVE interference it must be an odd number of half wavelengths, \(\Delta x = (2n - 1)\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\):

\(\dfrac{\lambda}{4} + (\mathrm{S_2P} - \mathrm{S_1P}) = (2n - 1)\dfrac{\lambda}{2} \Rightarrow \mathrm{S_2P} - \mathrm{S_1P} = (2n - 1)\dfrac{\lambda}{2} - \dfrac{\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}\left[4n - 3\right]\),  \(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

The effect of the \(\dfrac{\lambda}{4}\) introduced before the slits is simply to shift the whole fringe pattern sideways; the spacing of the fringes is unchanged.

(ii) With white light in place of the monochromatic source, the CENTRAL fringe stays WHITE, because at the centre the path difference is zero for every wavelength at once, so all the colours reinforce there. Away from the centre the fringe width \(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\) is proportional to wavelength, so each colour forms its maxima at a different place: a few coloured fringes appear on either side of the centre, violet nearest and red farthest out. Beyond those first few orders the maxima of some colours fall on the minima of others, the colours overlap completely, and the screen shows general white illumination with no distinguishable fringes.

rows.subtopic: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Model
rows.stem: Briefly explain Geiger-Marsden experiment. Show the variation of the number of particles scattered (N) with scattering angle \((\theta)\) in this experiment. What is the main conclusion that can be inferred from this plot ?
rows.solution:
The experiment. A narrow, collimated beam of alpha particles from a radioactive source was directed at a very thin gold foil, only about \(2{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-7}\) m thick, so that each alpha particle would meet essentially one layer of atoms. The alpha particles scattered by the foil were observed with a ROTATABLE detector consisting of a zinc sulphide screen and a microscope: an alpha particle striking the screen produced a brief flash of light, a scintillation, which could be seen and counted through the microscope. By swinging the detector round to different angles, the number of alpha particles scattered through each angle \(\theta\) was measured.

The variation to be shown. A plot of the number of scattered particles \(N\) against the scattering angle \(\theta\) (with \(N\) on a logarithmic scale, \(\theta\) running from \(0^\circ\) to \(180^\circ\)) falls extremely steeply. \(N\) is enormous for small angles and drops by several orders of magnitude as \(\theta\) increases, flattening into a very small but NON-ZERO tail at large angles, so that a few particles are scattered through more than \(90^\circ\) and a very few are turned almost straight back.

The main conclusion. Since the overwhelming majority of the alpha particles pass through almost undeviated, the atom must be mostly EMPTY space. But the few that are turned through very large angles must have met an intense concentrated repulsive force, which could only come from a very small region carrying the whole positive charge and practically the entire mass of the atom. That region is the NUCLEUS. The distance of closest approach of the most energetic alpha particles also puts an upper limit on its size.

rows.subtopic: Drift of Electrons and Resistivity
rows.stem:
(i) Define mobility of electrons. Give its SI units.
(ii) A steady current flows through a wire AB, as shown in the figure. What happens to the electric field and the drift velocity along the wire ? Justify your answer.
(iii) Consider the circuit shown in the figure. Find the effective resistance of the circuit and the current drawn from the battery.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — TWO printed figures, both load-bearing, and neither is described in the stem. (ii): a wire drawn hatched between end labels A on the left and B on the right, connected across a cell; described as a wire whose cross-section is not uniform along its length, with WITHHELD which end is the thicker, since 'what happens to the electric field and the drift velocity along the wire' turns entirely on that. (iii): the stem says only 'the circuit shown in the figure' — drawn is a network of five resistors labelled 10 \(\Omega\), 10 \(\Omega\), 30 \(\Omega\), 10 \(\Omega\) and 14 \(\Omega\) together with a 6 V battery; the TOPOLOGY is withheld because the effective resistance is exactly what is asked. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
(i) The mobility of an electron is the magnitude of the drift velocity it acquires per unit applied electric field:

\(\mu = \dfrac{|v_d|}{E}\).

Since the drift velocity produced by a field \(E\) is \(v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}\), where \(\tau\) is the relaxation time, this gives \(\mu = \dfrac{e\tau}{m}\), a property of the material alone.

SI unit: \(\mathrm{m^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\) (equivalently \(\mathrm{C\,s\,kg^{-1}}\)).

(ii) The figure shows a wire that is NOT of uniform cross-section: it is narrow at A and widens steadily towards B, so its area of cross-section increases from A to B. The current is steady, so by conservation of charge the same current \(I\) crosses every section of the wire.

Both quantities asked for therefore DECREASE from A to B.

Drift velocity: \(I = neAv_d\) gives \(v_d = \dfrac{I}{ne \times (\text{area})}\). The number density \(n\) and the charge \(e\) are the same throughout, and \(I\) is constant, so as the area grows the drift velocity falls.

Electric field: the current density is \(j = \dfrac{I}{\text{area}}\), which likewise falls, and \(E = \rho j = \dfrac{\rho I}{\text{area}}\) for a wire of resistivity \(\rho\). So the field falls in exactly the same proportion. This is consistent with \(v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}\): with \(e\), \(m\) and \(\tau\) fixed, the drift velocity and the field must rise and fall together.

So both the electric field and the drift velocity are largest at the narrow end A and decrease steadily along the wire towards the wide end B.

(iii) Read the network off the figure. Between the two terminals of the battery there are three separate paths:

the \(10\,\Omega\) at the top in series with the \(14\,\Omega\) on the right:  \(R_1 = 10 + 14 = 24\,\Omega\);

the middle \(10\,\Omega\) in series with the \(10\,\Omega\) below it:  \(R_2 = 10 + 10 = 20\,\Omega\);

the \(30\,\Omega\) on its own:  \(R_3 = 30\,\Omega\).

These three branches are connected in PARALLEL across the \(6\) V battery, so

\(\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{24} + \dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{5 + 6 + 4}{120} = \dfrac{15}{120} = \dfrac{1}{8}\),

giving an effective resistance

\(R = 8\,\Omega\).

The current drawn from the battery is then

\(I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{6}{8} = 0{\cdot}75\) A.

[Note on the marking scheme: beneath this working it prints 'Full credit of 1 1/2 marks is to be awarded for part (iii) even if a student does not attempt this part.' The Board therefore awarded part (iii) to every candidate irrespective of what was written. The working above is nevertheless the intended one and reaches the scheme's own values of \(8\,\Omega\) and \(0{\cdot}75\) A.]

rows.subtopic: Cells, EMF and Internal Resistance
rows.stem:
(i) Define electrical conductivity of a wire. Give its SI unit.
(ii) High current is to be drawn safely from (1) a low-voltage battery, and (2) a high-voltage battery. What can you say about the internal resistance of the two batteries ?
(iii) Calculate the total energy supplied by the batteries to the circuit shown in the figure, in one minute.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (iii) says only 'the circuit shown in the figure' and every value it needs is in the drawing. Described: a single closed loop carrying four resistors labelled 1 \(\Omega\), 2 \(\Omega\), 6 \(\Omega\) and 3 \(\Omega\) and two cells labelled 4 V and 10 V, with a current labelled I marked on the left-hand branch. Withheld: the two cells' relative polarity, which decides the net emf and therefore the energy supplied. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
(i) The electrical conductivity of a material is the reciprocal of its resistivity, \(\sigma = \dfrac{1}{\rho}\) — a measure of how readily the material lets a current pass. Equivalently it is defined by \(\vec{j} = \sigma\vec{E}\), the current density set up per unit applied electric field.

SI unit: \(\Omega^{-1}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), that is \(\mathrm{S\,m^{-1}}\) (siemens per metre).

(ii) The current a battery of emf \(\varepsilon\) and internal resistance \(r\) delivers to an external resistance \(R\) is \(I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R + r}\), and the largest it can ever be, with \(R = 0\), is \(I_{max} = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{r}\).

(1) Low-voltage battery. Here \(\varepsilon\) is small, so for \(I\) to be large the whole of \(R + r = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{I}\) must be small, and in particular the internal resistance must be VERY LOW. Otherwise most of the small emf is lost inside the cell itself and the high current is simply unobtainable. A car battery is the standard example: it is built with \(r\) of a fraction of an ohm precisely so that it can deliver hundreds of amperes at \(12\) V.

(2) High-voltage battery. Here \(\varepsilon\) is large, so \(\dfrac{\varepsilon}{I}\) is comparatively large and a high current can still be drawn even when \(r\) is sizeable. Safety then demands that the internal resistance be HIGH: if \(r\) were small, \(I_{max} = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{r}\) would be enormous, and an accidental short circuit across such a supply would deliver a lethal current. A large \(r\) limits the current to a safe value whatever is connected across the terminals.

So the low-voltage battery must have a low internal resistance, while the high-voltage battery should have a high one.

(iii) The circuit is a single loop, and the two cells are connected so that they OPPOSE each other, so the net emf driving the current is \(10 - 4 = 6\) V. The resistances in the loop total \(1 + 2 + 6 + 3 = 12\,\Omega\).

Applying Kirchhoff's loop rule, going round in the sense of \(I\):

\(10 - I \times 1 - 4 - 2I - 6I - 3I = 0\)

\(6 = 12I \Rightarrow I = 0{\cdot}5\) A.

The energy supplied to the circuit is the energy dissipated in its resistances, so in \(t = 60\) s:

\(H = I^2Rt = (0{\cdot}5)^2 \times 12 \times 60 = 0{\cdot}25 \times 12 \times 60 = 180\) J.

(Set out cell by cell, the \(10\) V cell delivers \(10 \times 0{\cdot}5 \times 60 = 300\) J while the \(4\) V cell, driven backwards by the larger one, absorbs \(4 \times 0{\cdot}5 \times 60 = 120\) J and is being charged. The net energy supplied to the circuit is \(300 - 120 = 180\) J, which is the same figure.)

rows.subtopic: Optical Instruments
rows.stem:
(i) Draw a ray diagram to show how the final image is formed at infinity in an astronomical refracting telescope. Obtain an expression for its magnifying power.
(ii) Two thin lenses \(\mathrm{L_1}\) and \(\mathrm{L_2}\), \(\mathrm{L_1}\) being a convex lens of focal length 24 cm and \(\mathrm{L_2}\) a concave lens of focal length 18 cm are placed coaxially at a separation of 45 cm. A 1 cm tall object is placed in front of the lens \(\mathrm{L_1}\) at a distance of 36 cm. Find the location and height of the image formed by the combination.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: the position of the final image in part (ii) is right but its HEIGHT is wrong. The scheme computes the magnification as (final image distance measured from \(\mathrm{L_1}\)) divided by (object distance from \(\mathrm{L_1}\)), \(\dfrac{-9}{-36} = \dfrac{1}{4}\), and reports an image \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) cm tall. The single-lens relation \(m = \dfrac{v}{u}\) cannot be applied across a two-lens system that way; the magnification of a combination is the PRODUCT of the individual magnifications, \(m_1 m_2 = (-2)(-2) = +4\), giving a \(4\) cm image. Tracing two rays right through both lenses confirms the image \(9\) cm to the left of \(\mathrm{L_1}\) with a height of \(+4\) cm.]

(i) Ray diagram to be drawn (normal adjustment, final image at infinity). Rays from a distant object arrive at the objective O as a parallel beam making a small angle \(\alpha\) with the principal axis. The objective, of large focal length \(f_o\), brings them to a real, inverted image \(\mathrm{A'B'}\) of height \(h\) in its focal plane. The eyepiece E, of small focal length \(f_e\), is placed so that this image lies exactly at ITS focus, which makes the tube length \(f_o + f_e\). The eyepiece therefore sends the light out as a parallel beam, so the final image is formed at infinity and the emergent beam makes an angle \(\beta\) with the axis. Arrows must be put on the rays to show the direction in which the light travels.

Magnifying power is the ratio of the angle the FINAL image subtends at the eye to the angle the OBJECT subtends at the unaided eye (here, at the objective):

\(m = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\).

Both angles are small, so each equals its own tangent, and from the diagram, with \(h\) the height of the intermediate image,

\(\alpha = \dfrac{h}{f_o}\)  and  \(\beta = \dfrac{h}{f_e}\).

Hence

\(m = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} = \dfrac{h/f_e}{h/f_o} = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\).

A telescope is therefore made powerful by giving the objective a long focal length and the eyepiece a short one.

(ii) Work through the two lenses in turn, applying \(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\) to each.

At the convex lens \(\mathrm{L_1}\):  \(f_1 = +24\) cm, \(u_1 = -36\) cm.

\(\dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{u_1} = \dfrac{1}{24} - \dfrac{1}{36} = \dfrac{3 - 2}{72} = \dfrac{1}{72} \Rightarrow v_1 = +72\) cm.

So \(\mathrm{L_1}\) alone would form a real image \(72\) cm to its right, with magnification

\(m_1 = \dfrac{v_1}{u_1} = \dfrac{72}{-36} = -2\)  (inverted, \(2\) cm tall).

At the concave lens \(\mathrm{L_2}\), which stands \(45\) cm from \(\mathrm{L_1}\): that image would lie \(72 - 45 = 27\) cm BEYOND \(\mathrm{L_2}\), so the light is converging towards it when it reaches \(\mathrm{L_2}\) and it acts as a VIRTUAL object, \(u_2 = +27\) cm, with \(f_2 = -18\) cm.

\(\dfrac{1}{v_2} = \dfrac{1}{f_2} + \dfrac{1}{u_2} = -\dfrac{1}{18} + \dfrac{1}{27} = \dfrac{-3 + 2}{54} = -\dfrac{1}{54} \Rightarrow v_2 = -54\) cm.

Location: the final image is \(54\) cm to the LEFT of \(\mathrm{L_2}\), that is \(54 - 45 = 9\) cm to the left of \(\mathrm{L_1}\) — on the same side as the object, so it is virtual.

Height: the magnification of the second lens is

\(m_2 = \dfrac{v_2}{u_2} = \dfrac{-54}{+27} = -2\),

and for a combination the magnifications MULTIPLY:

\(m = m_1 \times m_2 = (-2) \times (-2) = +4\).

So the height of the final image is \(4 \times 1 = 4\) cm, and the positive sign says it is erect with respect to the original object.

rows.subtopic: Refraction Through a Prism
rows.stem:
(i) Explain the working principle of an optical fibre with the help of a diagram. Mention one use of a light pipe.
(ii) A ray of light is incident at an angle of 60° on one face of a prism with the prism angle A = 60°. The ray passes symmetrically through the prism. Find the angle of minimum deviation \((\delta_m)\) and refractive index of the material of the prism. If the prism is immersed in water, how will \(\delta_m\) be affected ? Justify your answer.
rows.solution:
(i) Working principle of an optical fibre: TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION.

An optical fibre is a very fine thread with a central CORE of glass or plastic of high refractive index, surrounded by a CLADDING of slightly LOWER refractive index. Light fed in at one end travels almost along the axis, so it meets the core-cladding boundary at a large angle of incidence — greater than the critical angle for that pair of media. Going from the denser core to the rarer cladding, it is therefore totally internally reflected, with no refracted ray escaping and, unlike reflection at a mirror, with no loss of intensity. Striking the opposite boundary it is reflected again, and so on: the ray zig-zags down the fibre and is guided along it, following the fibre even where it is bent, until it emerges at the far end.

Diagram to be drawn: a long, gently curving fibre in section, the inner region labelled 'core, high \(n\)' and the outer sheath 'cladding, low \(n\)', with one ray entering at the left-hand face and zig-zagging between the two boundaries along the whole length before leaving at the right.

One use of a light pipe: in ENDOSCOPY, where a bundle of fibres carries light into an internal organ and brings the image back out for medical examination. (It is equally used for transmitting audio and video signals in optical communication.)

(ii) The ray passes SYMMETRICALLY through the prism, which is exactly the condition for minimum deviation: the angle of emergence equals the angle of incidence, \(e = i = 60^\circ\), and the refracted ray inside runs parallel to the base.

Angle of minimum deviation:

\(\delta_m = i + e - A = 60^\circ + 60^\circ - 60^\circ = 60^\circ\).

Refractive index, from the prism formula:

\(\mu = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{60^\circ + 60^\circ}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{60^\circ}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{\sin 60^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}/2}{1/2} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1{\cdot}73\).

Effect of immersing the prism in water. What governs the deviation is not the absolute refractive index of the glass but its index RELATIVE to the surrounding medium. In air that is \(\sqrt{3} \approx 1{\cdot}73\); in water it becomes

\(\mu_{rel} = \dfrac{\mu_{glass}}{\mu_{water}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4/3} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{4} \approx 1{\cdot}30\),

which is smaller. For a fixed prism angle \(A\), the relation above makes \(\mu\) an increasing function of \(\delta_m\); so a smaller \(\mu\) must correspond to a smaller \(\delta_m\). The angle of minimum deviation therefore DECREASES when the prism is immersed in water — the rays are bent less at each face because the two media are now closer in optical density.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem:
(i) A germanium crystal is doped with antimony. With the help of energy-band diagram, explain how the conductivity of the doped crystal is affected.
(ii) Briefly explain the two processes involved in the formation of a p-n junction.
(iii) What will the effect of (1) forward biasing, and (2) reverse biasing be on the width of depletion layer in a p-n junction diode ?
rows.solution:
(i) Germanium is tetravalent; antimony is PENTAVALENT, with five valence electrons. When an antimony atom replaces a germanium atom in the lattice, four of its five valence electrons form covalent bonds with the four neighbouring Ge atoms. The fifth electron finds no bond to enter and is held to its parent atom only very weakly.

In the energy-band picture this shows up as a DONOR level \(E_D\) lying just below the bottom of the conduction band \(E_C\). For germanium the gap \(E_C - E_D\) is only about \(0{\cdot}01\) eV, tiny compared with the band gap \(E_g \approx 0{\cdot}72\) eV of pure Ge. Thermal energy at room temperature (about \(0{\cdot}026\) eV) is more than enough to lift essentially every donor electron across that small step into the conduction band — and, importantly, it does so WITHOUT creating a hole in the valence band.

The number density of conduction electrons therefore becomes far greater than in the pure crystal, with \(n_e \gg n_h\), so the crystal is n-type. Since \(\sigma = e(n_e\mu_e + n_h\mu_h)\), the enormous increase in \(n_e\) makes the conductivity of the doped crystal very much LARGER than that of pure germanium.

Band diagram to be drawn: the valence band \(E_V\) shaded at the bottom, the conduction band \(E_C\) shaded at the top with the band gap \(E_g\) marked between them, and a dashed donor level \(E_D\) about \(0{\cdot}01\) eV below \(E_C\), with electrons shown in the conduction band and the valence band still nearly full.

(ii) The two processes are DIFFUSION and DRIFT.

Diffusion. Across the junction there is a steep concentration gradient: holes are the majority carriers on the p-side and electrons on the n-side. So holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side, and electrons diffuse from the n-side to the p-side. Each carrier that leaves takes its charge with it but leaves behind an IMMOBILE ionised impurity atom, so a layer of negative space charge builds up on the p-side of the junction and a layer of positive space charge on the n-side. That region, stripped of mobile carriers, is the depletion layer.

Drift. The space charge sets up an electric field across the depletion layer, directed from the n-side towards the p-side. This junction field sweeps any MINORITY carrier that strays into the region straight across: electrons from the p-side to the n-side, and holes from the n-side to the p-side. That motion under the field is the drift current, and it flows opposite to the diffusion current.

The junction settles down when the two exactly balance, so that no net current flows; the potential difference then standing across the depletion layer is the barrier potential.

(iii) (1) Forward biasing applies a field that OPPOSES the junction field, so the barrier potential is lowered and the depletion layer becomes THINNER — its width DECREASES.

(2) Reverse biasing applies a field in the SAME sense as the junction field, so the barrier potential is raised, more carriers are pulled back from the junction region, and the depletion layer becomes THICKER — its width INCREASES.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier
rows.stem:
(i) With the help of a circuit diagram, briefly explain the working of a full-wave rectifier using p-n junction diodes.
(ii) Draw V – I characteristics of a p-n junction diode. Explain how these characteristics make a diode suitable for rectification.
(iii) Carbon and silicon have the same lattice structure. Then why is carbon an insulator but silicon a semiconductor ?
rows.solution:
(i) Circuit. The a.c. input is applied to the primary of a CENTRE-TAP transformer. The two ends A and B of the secondary are connected to the p-sides of two diodes \(\mathrm{D_1}\) and \(\mathrm{D_2}\). The n-sides of the two diodes are joined together and taken to one end X of the load resistance \(R_L\); the other end Y of \(R_L\) is returned to the CENTRE TAP of the secondary. The output is taken across \(R_L\).

Working. Measured with respect to the centre tap, the voltages at A and at B are always in ANTIPHASE — when one end is positive the other is negative. During the half-cycle in which A is positive, \(\mathrm{D_1}\) is forward biased and conducts while \(\mathrm{D_2}\) is reverse biased and does not; the current flows out of A, through \(\mathrm{D_1}\), down through \(R_L\) from X to Y and back to the centre tap. During the next half-cycle the polarities reverse: \(\mathrm{D_2}\) conducts and \(\mathrm{D_1}\) is cut off, and the current flows out of B, through \(\mathrm{D_2}\), and again down through \(R_L\) from X to Y.

The essential point is that in BOTH halves of the input cycle the current through the load runs in the SAME direction. Both halves of the alternating input are therefore used — hence 'full-wave' — and the output across \(R_L\) is a unidirectional, pulsating voltage whose ripple frequency is twice the input frequency.

(ii) V-I characteristics to be drawn. Plot current against applied voltage with the FORWARD characteristic in the first quadrant, current in mA: it stays almost flat at nearly zero until the knee (threshold) voltage — about \(0{\cdot}3\) V for germanium, \(0{\cdot}7\) V for silicon — beyond which it rises very steeply. Plot the REVERSE characteristic in the third quadrant, current in \(\mu\)A: only a tiny, almost constant reverse saturation current flows, until the breakdown voltage is reached and the reverse current suddenly becomes large.

Why this suits it for rectification. The characteristic shows that the diode's resistance is very low in the forward direction and extremely high in the reverse direction, so it passes an appreciable current in ONE direction only. Connect it in series with an a.c. source and a load and it therefore conducts during the half-cycle that forward biases it and blocks during the half-cycle that reverse biases it. The alternating input is thus converted into a unidirectional output, which is precisely what rectification means.

(iii) Carbon and silicon do have the same tetrahedral lattice and the same four valence electrons, but those electrons sit in different shells: carbon's four bonding electrons are in the SECOND orbit, silicon's in the THIRD. The third shell is farther from the nucleus and is better screened by the inner closed shells, so silicon's valence electrons are held far less tightly and much less energy is needed to lift one of them into the conduction band.

This appears directly in the band gap: about \(5{\cdot}4\) eV for carbon in the diamond structure against about \(1{\cdot}1\) eV for silicon. Thermal energy at room temperature is of the order of \(0{\cdot}026\) eV, which can excite an appreciable number of electrons across silicon's modest gap, giving it enough free carriers to conduct weakly — a semiconductor. Carbon's gap is so wide that the number of electrons able to cross it is utterly negligible, so it has virtually no free carriers and behaves as an insulator.

[Note on the marking scheme: its printed sentence reads 'The 4 bonding of electrons of C and Si lie respectively, in the second and third orbit. Hence energy required to take out an electron from their atoms will be much less than that for C.' Taken literally that compares carbon with itself; the statement intended, and used above, is that the energy required is much less for Si than for C. The scheme's conclusion — that the number of free electrons available for conduction is significant in Si and negligible in C — is correct.]

rows.subtopic: Applications of Gauss's Law
rows.stem: Consider a uniformly charged thin conducting shell of radius R. Plot a graph showing the variation of \(|\vec{\mathrm{E}}|\) with distance r from the centre, for points \(0 \le r \le 3\mathrm{R}\).
rows.context: Electrostatics deals with the study of forces, fields and potentials arising from static charges. Force and electric field, due to a point charge is basically determined by Coulomb's law. For symmetric charge configurations, Gauss's law, which is also based on Coulomb's law, helps us to find the electric field. A charge/a system of charges like a dipole experience a force/torque in an electric field. Work is required to be done to provide a specific orientation to a dipole with respect to an electric field.
rows.solution:
Apply Gauss's law to a spherical Gaussian surface of radius \(r\) concentric with the shell. By symmetry \(\vec{E}\) is radial and of the same magnitude everywhere on that surface, so \(\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{S} = E \times 4\pi r^2 = \dfrac{q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}\).

For \(r < R\): all the charge of a CONDUCTING shell resides on its outer surface, so the Gaussian surface encloses no charge at all and

\(|\vec{E}| = 0\)  everywhere inside.

For \(r \ge R\): the surface encloses the whole charge \(Q\), so

\(|\vec{E}| = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{r^2}\),

exactly as though the entire charge were a point charge at the centre.

Graph to be drawn, \(|\vec{E}|\) against \(r\) for \(0 \le r \le 3R\): the curve runs flat along the \(r\)-axis at \(|\vec{E}| = 0\) from \(r = 0\) up to \(r = R\); at \(r = R\) it jumps DISCONTINUOUSLY to its maximum value \(\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{R^2}\) (mark that point with a dashed vertical line); and beyond \(r = R\) it falls away as \(\dfrac{1}{r^2}\), having dropped to one quarter of the peak at \(r = 2R\) and to one ninth of it at \(r = 3R\).

rows.subtopic: Electrostatic Potential due to Charges and Dipoles
rows.stem: The figure shows the variation of potential V with \(\dfrac{1}{r}\) for two point charges \(\mathrm{Q_1}\) and \(\mathrm{Q_2}\), where V is the potential at a distance r due to a point charge. Find \(\dfrac{\mathrm{Q_1}}{\mathrm{Q_2}}\).
rows.context: Electrostatics deals with the study of forces, fields and potentials arising from static charges. Force and electric field, due to a point charge is basically determined by Coulomb's law. For symmetric charge configurations, Gauss's law, which is also based on Coulomb's law, helps us to find the electric field. A charge/a system of charges like a dipole experience a force/torque in an electric field. Work is required to be done to provide a specific orientation to a dipole with respect to an electric field.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the only quantities the ratio can be computed from are the two angles printed in the drawing; the stem states neither. Described: a pair of axes, vertical axis V, horizontal axis \(\dfrac{1}{r}\), origin marked O, and two straight lines drawn from the origin, labelled \(\mathrm{Q_1}\) and \(\mathrm{Q_2}\), each with the angle it makes to the horizontal axis marked. Withheld: the two angle values, since \(\mathrm{Q_1}/\mathrm{Q_2}\) is the ratio of their tangents. Page idx 24.
rows.solution:
The potential at a distance \(r\) from a point charge \(Q\) is

\(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{r} = \left(\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\right)\dfrac{1}{r}\).

So \(V\) is directly proportional to \(\dfrac{1}{r}\), and a graph of \(V\) against \(\dfrac{1}{r}\) is a straight line through the origin whose SLOPE is \(\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\) — that is, the slope is proportional to the charge. Both lines in the figure do pass through the origin, as they must.

Taking the ratio, the constant \(\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\) cancels and only the slopes are left.
