The slope of each line is the tangent of the angle it makes with the \(\dfrac{1}{r}\) axis, and the figure marks those angles as \(60^\circ\) for \(\mathrm{Q_1}\) and \(30^\circ\) for \(\mathrm{Q_2}\):

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{Q_1}}{\mathrm{Q_2}} = \dfrac{\tan 60^\circ}{\tan 30^\circ} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{1/\sqrt{3}} = 3\).

So \(\dfrac{\mathrm{Q_1}}{\mathrm{Q_2}} = 3\): the steeper line belongs to the charge three times the larger.

rows.subtopic: Electric Dipole and Dipole in a Uniform Field
rows.stem: An electric dipole of dipole moment of \(6 \times 10^{-7}\) C-m is kept in a uniform electric field of \(10^4\) N/C such that the dipole moment and the electric field are parallel. Calculate the potential energy of the dipole.
rows.context: Electrostatics deals with the study of forces, fields and potentials arising from static charges. Force and electric field, due to a point charge is basically determined by Coulomb's law. For symmetric charge configurations, Gauss's law, which is also based on Coulomb's law, helps us to find the electric field. A charge/a system of charges like a dipole experience a force/torque in an electric field. Work is required to be done to provide a specific orientation to a dipole with respect to an electric field.
rows.solution:
The potential energy of a dipole of moment \(\vec{p}\) placed in a uniform field \(\vec{E}\) is

\(U = -\vec{p} \cdot \vec{E} = -pE\cos\theta\),

where \(\theta\) is the angle between the dipole moment and the field, measured from the orientation in which they are parallel.

Here the dipole moment and the electric field are stated to be PARALLEL, so \(\theta = 0^\circ\) and \(\cos\theta = 1\). With \(p = 6 \times 10^{-7}\) C-m and \(E = 10^4\) N/C:

\(U = -pE = -\left(6 \times 10^{-7}\right) \times \left(10^4\right)\)

\(U = -6 \times 10^{-3}\) J.

The value is negative and is the LEAST that \(U\) can take for this dipole in this field, because \(-pE\cos\theta\) is a minimum at \(\theta = 0\). That orientation, with the dipole aligned along the field, is therefore the position of stable equilibrium.

rows.subtopic: Electric Dipole and Dipole in a Uniform Field
rows.stem: An electric dipole of dipole moment \(\vec{p}\) is initially kept in a uniform electric field \(\vec{E}\) such that \(\vec{p}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{E}\). Find the amount of work done in rotating the dipole to a position at which \(\vec{p}\) becomes antiparallel to \(\vec{E}\).
rows.context: Electrostatics deals with the study of forces, fields and potentials arising from static charges. Force and electric field, due to a point charge is basically determined by Coulomb's law. For symmetric charge configurations, Gauss's law, which is also based on Coulomb's law, helps us to find the electric field. A charge/a system of charges like a dipole experience a force/torque in an electric field. Work is required to be done to provide a specific orientation to a dipole with respect to an electric field.
rows.solution:
The work done in rotating a dipole in a uniform field, against the torque of the field, equals the increase in its potential energy. With \(U(\theta) = -pE\cos\theta\),

\(W = U(\theta_2) - U(\theta_1) = -pE\cos\theta_2 - \left(-pE\cos\theta_1\right) = -pE\left(\cos\theta_2 - \cos\theta_1\right)\).

(The same result follows by integrating the torque: \(W = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} pE\sin\theta\,d\theta\).)

The dipole starts PERPENDICULAR to the field, so \(\theta_1 = 90^\circ\), and finishes ANTIPARALLEL to it, so \(\theta_2 = 180^\circ\). Substituting:

\(W = -pE\left(\cos 180^\circ - \cos 90^\circ\right) = -pE\left(-1 - 0\right)\)

\(W = +pE\).

So the work that must be done is \(pE\), and it is positive because the dipole is being turned away from the field and towards the antiparallel orientation, which is the position of MAXIMUM potential energy and of unstable equilibrium.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: How will the power of a lens be affected with an increase of wavelength of light ?
rows.context: The lens maker's formula is useful to design lenses of desired focal lengths using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature. The focal length also depends on the refractive index of the material of the lens and the surrounding medium. The refractive index depends on the wavelength of the light used. The power of a lens is related to its focal length.
rows.solution:
By the lens maker's formula the power of a thin lens is

\(P = \dfrac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)\).

For a given lens the radii \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) are fixed, so the bracket is a constant and \(P\) is proportional to \((\mu - 1)\). Everything therefore turns on how the refractive index of the material varies with wavelength.

The refractive index of a transparent medium DECREASES as the wavelength increases — that is the dispersion which makes a prism spread white light, with \(\mu\) largest for violet and smallest for red. (Cauchy's relation \(\mu = A + \dfrac{B}{\lambda^2}\) shows the same thing.)

So increasing the wavelength decreases \(\mu\), hence decreases \((\mu - 1)\), hence decreases \(P\). The POWER of the lens therefore DECREASES as the wavelength of the light is increased, which is the same as saying its focal length increases: a lens converges red light less strongly than violet.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: The radius of curvature of two surfaces of a convex lens is R each. For what value of \(\mu\) of its material will its focal length become equal to R ?
rows.context: The lens maker's formula is useful to design lenses of desired focal lengths using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature. The focal length also depends on the refractive index of the material of the lens and the surrounding medium. The refractive index depends on the wavelength of the light used. The power of a lens is related to its focal length.
rows.solution:
For a biconvex lens whose two surfaces both have radius of curvature \(R\), the sign convention makes the first surface convex towards the incoming light and the second concave towards it:

\(R_1 = +R\)  and  \(R_2 = -R\).

Substituting in the lens maker's formula,

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right) = (\mu - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{-1}{R}\right) = (\mu - 1)\dfrac{2}{R}\).

The focal length is required to be equal to \(R\), so put \(f = R\):

\(\dfrac{1}{R} = (\mu - 1)\dfrac{2}{R} \Rightarrow 1 = 2(\mu - 1) \Rightarrow \mu - 1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

Hence

\(\mu = \dfrac{3}{2} = 1{\cdot}5\).

So a material of refractive index \(1{\cdot}5\) gives such a lens a focal length equal to the radius of curvature of its faces.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: The focal length of a concave lens of \(\mu = 1{\cdot}5\) is 20 cm in air. It is completely immersed in water of \(\mu = \dfrac{4}{3}\). Calculate its focal length in water.
rows.context: The lens maker's formula is useful to design lenses of desired focal lengths using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature. The focal length also depends on the refractive index of the material of the lens and the surrounding medium. The refractive index depends on the wavelength of the light used. The power of a lens is related to its focal length.
rows.solution:
Write the lens maker's formula in each medium. The geometrical factor \(\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)\) is a property of the lens alone and is the SAME in both, so it can be eliminated by dividing.

In air, the refractive index of the glass relative to its surroundings is \(\mu = 1{\cdot}5\):

\(\dfrac{1}{f_{air}} = (1{\cdot}5 - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)\).

In water the relevant index is that of the glass RELATIVE to water:

\(\mu_{rel} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{4/3} = \dfrac{9}{8}\),

so

\(\dfrac{1}{f_{water}} = \left(\dfrac{9}{8} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{8}\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)\).

Dividing the first by the second:

\(\dfrac{f_{water}}{f_{air}} = \dfrac{1/2}{1/8} = 4\).

Hence

\(f_{water} = 4 \times f_{air} = 4 \times 20 = 80\) cm.

So the focal length in water is \(80\) cm, four times its value in air. The lens is still a DIVERGING one — in the full sign convention its focal length goes from \(-20\) cm to \(-80\) cm — but it is much weaker, because the refractive index of the glass relative to water is far closer to \(1\) than its index relative to air, so each surface bends the light much less.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: An object is placed in front of a lens which forms its erect image of magnification 3. The power of the lens is 5 D. Calculate the distance of the object and the image from the lens.
rows.context: The lens maker's formula is useful to design lenses of desired focal lengths using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature. The focal length also depends on the refractive index of the material of the lens and the surrounding medium. The refractive index depends on the wavelength of the light used. The power of a lens is related to its focal length.
rows.solution:
The image is ERECT and three times the size of the object, so the magnification is positive:

\(m = +3 = \dfrac{v}{u} \Rightarrow v = 3u\).

The focal length follows from the power:

\(f = \dfrac{100}{P}\,\mathrm{cm} = \dfrac{100}{+5} = +20\) cm,

so the lens is convex. (A convex lens does form an erect, magnified, virtual image when the object is nearer than the focus, which is the situation here.)

Substituting in the lens equation \(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{3u} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{20}\)

\(\dfrac{1 - 3}{3u} = \dfrac{1}{20} \Rightarrow \dfrac{-2}{3u} = \dfrac{1}{20} \Rightarrow 3u = -40\)

\(u = -\dfrac{40}{3}\,\mathrm{cm} \approx -13{\cdot}3\) cm,

and then

\(v = 3u = -40\) cm.

So the object stands \(\dfrac{40}{3} \approx 13{\cdot}3\) cm in front of the lens — inside the focal length of \(20\) cm, as it must be — and the image is \(40\) cm from the lens on the SAME side as the object. The negative sign for \(v\) confirms that the image is virtual, and it is erect and magnified three times, as required.
